summary: This informational document considers how pervasive encryption affects network operators. RFC 7258 discusses the need to protect users' privacy, and making networks unmanageable is not a goal. It looks at how widespread encryption changes common operator practices.

plainLanguage.summary: Encrypting traffic protects the people sending it, but it also hides the traffic from the people running the network. This document lists what network operators lose as more traffic becomes encrypted, and what they might do instead.

questions: how does encryption affect network operators
what are the effects of pervasive encryption
how does encryption affect network troubleshooting
subtitle: How widespread encryption affects network operators' ability to manage, optimize, and secure networks.

tldr.problem: Network operations grew up in a world where most traffic was readable, and much of the toolchain depends on being able to look inside it.
tldr.mechanism: The document surveys what operators do with visible traffic, from traffic surveys and troubleshooting to load balancing, content filtering and accounting, and notes what each practice loses as more traffic is encrypted.
tldr.outcome: It is a survey rather than a proposal: the authors say operators support strong encryption, and the aim is to identify new work that lets the same goals be met without operators seeing the session data.

today: RFC 8404 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the operational community's catalogue of what pervasive encryption costs network operators. It has no IANA actions, and it says that its authors do not endorse the practices it describes, some of which it notes have been considered controversial or contrary to earlier IETF statements.

sections.title: The Tension Between Privacy and Manageability
sections.content:
In response to the pervasive monitoring revelations and the IETF consensus that pervasive monitoring is an attack, efforts are under way to increase the encryption of Internet traffic. Pervasive monitoring is of serious concern to users, operators and application providers. RFC 7258 discusses the critical need to protect users' privacy when developing IETF specifications, and also recognises that making networks unmanageable to mitigate pervasive monitoring is not an acceptable outcome; rather, an appropriate balance would emerge over time.

This document describes practices currently used by network operators to manage, operate and secure their networks, and how those practices may be impacted by a shift to increased use of encryption. It provides operators' perspectives about the motivations and objectives of those practices as well as the effects anticipated by operators as use of encryption increases. It is a summary of concerns of the operational community as they transition to managing networks with less visibility. It does not endorse the use of the practices described, nor does it aim to provide a comprehensive treatment of the effects of current practices, some of which have been considered controversial or contradictory to previous IETF statements. Several RFCs consider the end-to-end architectural principle to be a guiding principle for the development of Internet protocols.

The goal is to help inform future protocol development so that operational impact is part of the conversation, and perhaps new methods could be developed to accomplish some of the goals of current practices despite changes in the extent to which cleartext will be available to network operators. Traditional network management, planning, security operations and performance optimization were developed on an Internet where a large majority of data traffic flowed without encryption. While unencrypted traffic made information that aids operations and troubleshooting at all layers accessible, it also made pervasive monitoring by unseen parties possible. With broad support and increased awareness of the need to consider privacy, it is important to catalog existing management, operational and security practices that depend on the availability of cleartext and to explore whether critical operational practices can be met by less invasive means.

The document refers to several forms of service provider. Network service providers, or network operators, provide IP packet transport primarily, though they may bundle other services. Application service providers primarily offer systems that participate as an endpoint in communications with the application user. Hosting service providers lease computing, storage and communications systems in data centres. In practice many companies perform two or more of these roles but may be historically associated with one.

Pervasive encryption in this document refers to all types of session encryption including TLS, IPsec, QUIC and others that are increasingly deployed. Session encryption helps to prevent both passive and active attacks on transport protocols. Active attacks have long been a motivation for increased encryption, and preventing pervasive monitoring became a focus just a few years ago; the Internet Architecture Board released a statement advocating increased use of encryption in November 2014. Perspectives on encryption paradigms have shifted over time to make ease of deployment a high priority and to balance that against providing the maximum possible level of security. One such shift is Opportunistic Security, which suggests that when use of authenticated encryption is not possible, cleartext sessions should be upgraded to unauthenticated session encryption rather than no encryption; it encourages upgrading from cleartext but cannot require or guarantee such upgrades.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a real tension: the IETF has said both that user privacy matters and that networks must stay manageable. This document is the operators' side of that argument, and it aims to push the conversation towards new ways of meeting the same goals.

sections.title: What Operators Do With Readable Traffic
sections.content:
Service providers use various techniques to operate, manage and secure their networks. The document details the purpose of several techniques and which protocol fields are used to accomplish each task, noting that in response to increased encryption some providers may be tempted to undertake undesirable security practices in order to regain access to those fields, and that new methods could be developed to accomplish the same goals without providers having to see session data.

Traffic surveys. Internet traffic surveys are useful in many pursuits, such as input for studies of internet traffic analysis, network planning and optimisation. Tracking trends in traffic growth has relied on a view of traffic composition with a particular level of assumed accuracy, based on access to cleartext. Passive monitoring makes inferences using the maximal information available and is subject to inaccuracies from incomplete sampling or loss due to monitoring-system overload. When encryption conceals more layers in each packet, reliance on pattern inferences and other heuristics grows and accuracy suffers: the traffic patterns between server and browser depend on browser supplier and version, even when the sessions use the same server application.

Troubleshooting. Network operators use protocol-dissecting analysers when responding to customer problems, to identify the presence of attack traffic, and to identify root causes such as misconfiguration. In limited cases packet captures may also be used when a customer approves of access to their packets or provides captures close to the endpoint. Protocol dissection is generally limited to supporting protocols such as DNS and DHCP, network and transport protocols such as IP and TCP, and some higher-layer protocols such as RTP and RTCP. Troubleshooting will move closer to the endpoint with increased encryption, and troubleshooting effectively using a 5-tuple may require education. Operators are often the first ones called upon to investigate application problems, and the ability to identify the problem application's traffic is important; IP address filtering is not useful for applications using content delivery networks or cloud providers. By investigating packet loss from TCP sequence and acknowledgement numbers, round-trip time from TCP timestamp options or application-layer transactions such as DNS or HTTP response time, TCP receive-window size, packet corruption from checksum verification, inefficient fragmentation, or application-layer problems, the operator can narrow the problem to a portion of the network, server overload, or client and server misconfiguration. In many instances the exposed packet header is sufficient for this kind of troubleshooting.

When increased encryption is used, operators lose a source of data that may be used to debug user issues: IPsec obscures TCP and RTP header information while TLS and SRTP do not, so application-server operators using increased encryption might be called upon more frequently to assist with debugging. It may be possible to continue transaction-monitoring activities without cleartext access to the application layers of interest, but inaccuracy will increase and efficiency of repair activities will decrease, because an application-protocol error or failure would be opaque to network troubleshooters when transport encryption is applied. Repair time directly reduces the availability of the service, and most network operators have made availability a key metric in their service level agreements.

Traffic-analysis fingerprinting. Fingerprinting is used in traffic analysis and monitoring to identify traffic streams that match certain patterns, and this technique can be used with both cleartext and encrypted sessions.

Load balancers. A standalone load balancer is one you can take off the shelf, place in front of a pool of servers and configure, and it will balance traffic among the servers. Standalone load balancers rely on the plainly observable information in the packets they forward, typically a 5-tuple, and this configuration terminates TLS sessions at the load balancer, making it the endpoint instead of the server. An integrated load balancer is developed as an integral part of the service provided by the server pool, and can communicate state with the pool to route flows to the appropriate servers. For high availability it is important that when packets belonging to a flow start to arrive at a different load balancer in the pool, they continue to be forwarded to the original server. Mobile operators deploy integrated load balancers to assist with maintaining connection state as devices migrate, and anycast services typically employed by large content owners face an additional challenge: a migration to a different network in the middle of a connection greatly increases the chances of packets being routed to a different anycast point of presence, and the load balancer there, potentially thousands of miles away, would not have information about the new flow. This has led to practices of intercepting TLS in front of load balancers to regain visibility, at a cost to security and privacy. An area for further research includes end-to-end solutions that provide a simpler architecture and may solve the issue with CDN anycast, in which connections would be migrated to a CDN unicast address.

Content filtering. Service providers might block content to comply with requests from law enforcement or regulatory authorities, to effectuate parental controls, to enforce content-based billing, or for other reasons. A proxy is installed that analyses the transport metadata of the content users are viewing and filters content based on either a blacklist of sites or the user's predefined profile. One commonly used method involves a trigger based on the proxy identifying a DNS lookup of a host name in a URL that appears on a blacklist, so that subsequent requests to that domain are rerouted to a proxy that checks whether the full URL matches a blocked URL and returns a 404 if it matches. This technique does not work where DNS traffic is encrypted. Content filtering via a proxy can also use an intercepting certificate where the client's session is terminated at the proxy, which is an opt-in strategy where the endpoint is configured to trust the intercepting certificate; changes to TLS 1.3 do not impact this more invasive method of interception, which has the potential to expose every HTTPS session to an active man in the middle. Parental control, where some users are deliberately denied access to age-sensitive content as a feature, may use more granular application-layer metadata, and methods that accessed cleartext application-layer metadata no longer work when sessions are encrypted.

Network access and data usage. When the requested service is about to consume the remainder of a user's plan limits, the transmission could be terminated and advance notifications sent to the user. Some providers redirect the customer using an HTTP redirect to a captive portal page explaining the reason for the blockage. When the HTTP headers and content are encrypted, this appropriately prevents carriers from intercepting the traffic and performing an HTTP redirect; as a result, some mobile carriers block customers' encrypted requests, and the customer may need to call customer care to find out the reason, possibly extending the time needed to restore their network access. While well-deployed SMS-based solutions exist that do not involve out-of-specification protocol interception, this remains an unsolved problem for non-SMS users.
sections.plainLanguage: The document walks through the operator's tool bag: measuring what the traffic is, finding out why a call is choppy, spreading load across servers, blocking what must be blocked, and enforcing data limits. Each one leans on being able to read the traffic, and each one loses something when the traffic is encrypted.

sections.title: Hosting Providers and Enterprises
sections.content:
In hosting and application service provider environments, the operator and the customer are often closer together, and the practices differ accordingly. Management-access security is the first concern: the host needs to reach the machines it runs, and the customer needs to know that nobody else can. Monitoring customer access means watching how the hosted systems are being used, which overlaps with the host's own operational interest in knowing what is running. SP content monitoring of applications is the case where the provider inspects the applications it hosts, for example to enforce acceptable use, and the document notes that this is one of the areas where the boundary between the provider and the customer is least clear and where the provider has the most ability to act.

For hosted applications, the document describes monitoring of managed applications, where the provider watches the behaviour of software it operates on the customer's behalf, and mail service providers, where the provider has to make judgements about the content of the mail it carries and about the senders it accepts, and where reputation systems and feedback loops are central to those judgements.

On data storage, the document covers object-level encryption, where the stored data is encrypted per object rather than per disk, disk encryption and data at rest, and cross-data-centre replication services, where the copies of data held in different places are a further place where access controls have to be thought about.

For enterprises, the document describes the monitoring practices of the enterprise itself: security monitoring within the enterprise, where the goal is to detect an attacker inside rather than outside; monitoring application performance in the enterprise; and diagnostics and troubleshooting for enterprise networks, where the organisation is both the user and the operator and therefore has more freedom about what to encrypt and what to leave readable. It then sets out techniques for monitoring internet-session traffic from inside the enterprise, where the enterprise may be able to see traffic to and from its own services, and notes that the same techniques used to attack can be used to defend, which is a theme that runs through the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The closer the operator is to the application, the more the operator can still see. A hosting provider sits on the machine and can look at what it runs; an enterprise can watch its own users; both are in a different position from a network operator in the middle of the Internet.

sections.title: Security Monitoring for Specific Attacks
sections.content:
The document goes through the attack types that operators monitor for and asks what changes for each. Mail abuse and spam rely heavily on inspecting message content and on reputation data about the sending infrastructure; the reputation side survives encryption, the content side does not. Denial of service detection relies on seeing traffic volumes and patterns, which encryption does not hide, but mitigation that depends on understanding the traffic is harder. Phishing detection has traditionally relied on inspecting links and page content, so it is among the practices most affected, and the document discusses the move towards signals such as key transparency, which put trust information outside the encrypted session. Botnets are tracked by the addresses and infrastructure they use, much of which is visible in the transport headers, so tracking survives but acting on individual sessions does not. Malware detection has relied on inspecting payloads and on reputation lists, and the document notes that the move of operators towards blocking known bad addresses and towards sinkholing has partly compensated. Spoofed-source IP address protection is the exception that encryption does not affect, because the source address is in the outer header and is not protected by the session encryption.

The section ends with a call for further work, because the techniques that remain available are not sufficient on their own and the security community has to find new ways to detect and mitigate attacks when the payload cannot be read.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the ways of spotting an attack relied on reading the traffic, so they weaken as encryption spreads. Tracking the addresses and infrastructure behind an attack still works; the address of the packet itself is not encrypted.

sections.title: What a Network Can Still See
sections.content:
The document describes specific techniques used in monitoring applications that are visible to the network if a 5-tuple is exposed, and includes an overview of IP Flow Information Export, a flow-based protocol used to export information about network flows.

IPFIX. Many of the accounting, monitoring and measurement tasks described in the document use IPFIX for export and storage of the monitored information. IPFIX evolved from the widely deployed NetFlow protocol, which exports information about flows identified by 5-tuple. While NetFlow was largely concerned with exporting per-flow byte and packet counts for accounting purposes, IPFIX's extensible Information Model provides a variety of Information Elements for representing information above and below the traditional network-layer flow information, and enterprise-specific elements allow exporter vendors to define their own, many of which are driven by header and payload inspection at the metering process. The deployment of encryption has no direct effect on the use of IPFIX, but certain defined elements may become unavailable when the metering process cannot decrypt former cleartext information: HTTPS renders HTTP header analysis impossible, so elements derived from the header, such as the content type or the user agent, cannot be exported. The collection of IPFIX data provides a point of centralisation for information that is potentially business and privacy critical; the file format specification recommends encryption for this data at rest, and the IP Flow Anonymization specification defines a metadata format for describing the anonymization functions applied to an IPFIX dataset if anonymization is employed for data sharing.

TLS Server Name Indication. When initiating the TLS handshake, the client may provide an extension field that indicates the server to which it is attempting a secure connection. It was standardised in 2003 to enable servers to present the correct certificate to clients in a deployment of multiple virtual servers hosted by the same infrastructure and IP address. Although it is optional, it is supported by all modern browsers, web servers and developer libraries, and one provider reports that many of their customers see client usage of the extension over 99%. Existing network filters that examine a client hello for the extension cannot expect to always find one, and work on encrypting it has been adopted by the TLS Working Group, so there will be an option to encrypt it in future versions. The per-domain nature of the extension may not reveal the specific service or media type being accessed: certain blog or social network feeds may be deemed adult content, but the extension will only indicate the server domain rather than a path.

Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation. ALPN is a TLS extension that may be used to indicate the application protocol within the session. It is likely to be of more value to the network where it indicates a protocol dedicated to a particular traffic type, such as video streaming, rather than a multi-use protocol. It is used as part of HTTP/2 but will not indicate the traffic types that make up streams within a multiplex. ALPN is sent in cleartext in the client hello, and the server returns it in encrypted extensions in TLS 1.3.

Content length, bitrate and pacing. The content length of encrypted traffic is effectively the same as that of the cleartext, since block ciphers use padding but this makes a negligible difference. Bitrate and pacing are generally application specific and do not change much when the content is encrypted, although multiplexed formats such as HTTP/2 and QUIC may incorporate several application streams over one connection, which makes the bitrate no longer application specific. Packet padding is available in HTTP/2, TLS 1.3 and many other protocols, and traffic analysis is made more difficult by such countermeasures.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption hides the message, not the envelope. The network can still see which addresses are talking, roughly how much data is moving, which server name was asked for, and which application protocol was agreed. Those are the signals a future management approach would have to live with.

sections.title: Where the Document Wants Things to Go
sections.content:
As stated in RFC 7258, an appropriate balance between network management and pervasive monitoring mitigations will emerge over time as real instances of this tension are considered. Numerous operators made it clear in their response to this document that they fully support strong encryption and providing privacy for end users, and that this is a common goal. Operators recognise that not all the practices documented need to be supported going forward, either because of the risk to end-user privacy or because alternate technologies and tools have already emerged.

The document is intended to support network engineers and other innovators in working towards solving network and security management problems with protocol designers and application developers in new ways that facilitate adoption of strong encryption rather than preventing the use of encryption. By having the discussions on network and security management practices with application developers and protocol designers, each side of the debate can understand the other's goals, work towards alternate solutions, and drop practices that should no longer be supported. A goal of the document is to assist the IETF in understanding some of the current practices so as to identify new work items for IETF-related use cases that can facilitate the adoption of strong session encryption and support network and security management. The document adds no new security considerations, as it is a summary and includes no new protocol or functionality, and it has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators say plainly that they want strong encryption too. The document's job is to describe what has to be reinvented so that protecting the user's traffic does not mean giving up on running the network.

viz.caption: The operator practices the document surveys

items.title: Traffic surveys
items.text: Studying what the traffic on the network is, to plan and to track trends. Accuracy falls as more layers are hidden and guesses are needed.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Dissecting protocols to find the cause of a customer problem. With encryption, the diagnosis moves closer to the endpoint.

items.title: Fingerprinting
items.text: Identifying traffic streams by their patterns. Works with encrypted sessions as well as cleartext ones.

items.title: Load balancing
items.text: Spreading connections across a pool of servers. Session state has to be visible, so TLS is often terminated at the balancer.

items.title: Differential treatment
items.text: Treating different applications differently, for example in cellular radio networks where capacity is scarce.

items.title: Content filtering
items.text: Blocking sites on a blacklist, or blocking by the user's own profile. DNS-based blocking stops working when DNS is encrypted.

items.title: Accounting and data limits
items.text: Charging for data and stopping users at their plan limit, often with a redirect to a page explaining why.

items.title: Performance proxies
items.text: Middleboxes that speed up delivery by working on the traffic. These need to read and rewrite it.

viz.caption: What a network can still learn once sessions are encrypted

cells: Which addresses and ports are talking.
Still visible; it is outside the encrypted session.
Which server the client asked for. Standardised in 2003 and used by over 99% of one provider's customers.
Still sent in the clear, but it is optional and there is now work on encrypting it.
Which application protocol was agreed, such as a video streaming protocol.
Sent in the clear in the client hello; the server returns it inside the encrypted extensions in TLS 1.3.
Effectively unchanged; block cipher padding makes a negligible difference.
Generally unchanged, except where several application streams share one connection.
The content type, the user agent, the path requested.
Not available, which means the IPFIX elements derived from them cannot be exported.

viz.caption: How the attack types the document covers are affected

items.title: Mail abuse and spam
items.text: Reputation data about sending infrastructure survives; inspecting the message body does not.

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: Volumes and patterns stay visible; mitigation that depends on understanding the traffic is harder.

items.title: Phishing
items.text: Relied on inspecting links and page content, so it is among the most affected, prompting work on trust signals outside the session.

items.title: Botnets
items.text: Tracking the addresses and infrastructure behind a botnet survives; acting on individual sessions does not.

items.title: Malware
items.text: Payload inspection is lost, partly compensated by blocking known bad addresses and by sinkholing.

items.title: Spoofed source addresses
items.text: Unaffected, because the source address sits in the outer header and is not part of the encrypted session.
